{{Short description|Special tangential structure}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Spin<sup>c</sup> structure}}

In [[spin geometry]], a '''spin<sup>c</sup> structure''' (or '''complex spin structure''') is a generalization of a [[spin structure]]. In mathematics, these are used to describe [[Spinor bundle|spinor bundles]] and [[Spinor|spinors]], which in physics are used to describe [[Spin (physics)|spin]], an intrinsic [[angular momentum]] of [[Particle|particles]] after which they have been named. Since spin<sup>c</sup> structures also exist under weakened conditions, which might not allow spin structures, they provide a suitable alternative for such situations. [[Orientability|Orientable]] manifolds with a spin<sup>c</sup> structure are called '''spin<sup>c</sup> manifolds'''.<ref>Lawson & Michelson 90, Definition D.3</ref> C stands for the [[Complex number|complex numbers]], which are denoted <math>\mathbb{C}</math> and appear in the definition of the underlying [[Spinc group|spin<sup>c</sup> group]].

In four dimensions, a spin<sup>c</sup> structure defines two complex plane bundles, which can be used to describe negative and positive [[Chirality (physics)|chirality]] of [[Spinor|spinors]], for example in the [[Dirac equation]] of [[relativistic quantum field theory]]. Another central application is [[Seiberg–Witten theory]], which uses them to study [[4-manifold|4-manifolds]].

== Definition ==
Let <math>M</math> be a <math>n</math>-dimensional [[orientable manifold]]. Its [[tangent bundle]] <math>TM</math> is described by a classifying map <math>M\rightarrow\operatorname{BSO}(n)</math> into the [[Classifying space for SO(n)|classifying space]] <math>\operatorname{BSO}(n)</math> of the [[special orthogonal group]] <math>\operatorname{SO}(n)</math>. It can factor over the map <math>\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}(n)\rightarrow\operatorname{BSO}(n)</math> induced by the canonical projection <math>\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(n)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{SO}(n)</math> on [[Classifying space|classifying spaces]]. In this case, the classifying map lifts to a continuous map <math>M\rightarrow\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}(n)</math> into the classifying space <math>\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}(n)</math> of the [[Spinc group|spin<sup>c</sup> group]] <math>\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(n)</math>. Its [[homotopy]] class is called ''spin<sup>c</sup> structure''.<ref>Albanese & Milivojević 2021, Definition 3.1</ref><ref>''Stable complex and Spin<sup>c</sup>-structures'', Definition D.28</ref>

Assume <math>M</math> has a spin<sup>c</sup> structure. Let then <math>\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(M)</math> denote the set of spin<sup>c</sup> structures on <math>M</math>. The first [[unitary group]] [[Principal U(1)-bundle|<math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>]] is the second factor of the spin<sup>c</sup> group and using its [[Classifying space for U(n)|classifying space]] [[Principal U(1)-bundle|<math>\operatorname{BU}(1)
\cong\operatorname{BSO}(2)</math>]], which is the infinite [[complex projective space]] [[Principal U(1)-bundle|<math>\mathbb{C}P^\infty</math>]] and a model of the [[Eilenberg–MacLane space]] <math>K(\mathbb{Z},2)</math>, there is a [[bijection]]:<ref>Mellor 1995, Theorem 5</ref>

: <math>\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(M)
\cong[M,\operatorname{BU}(1)]
\cong[M,\mathbb{C}P^\infty]
\cong[M,K(\mathbb{Z},2)]
\cong H^2(M,\mathbb{Z}).</math>

The former isomorphism follows from the [[Puppe sequence]] for the fibration <math>\mathbb{C}P^\infty\hookrightarrow\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}(n)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{BSO}(n)</math> (when applying [[Principal U(1)-bundle|<math>[M,-]</math>]]).<ref>Albanese & Milivojević 2021, p. 6</ref>

Due to the canonical projection <math>\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}(n)\rightarrow\operatorname{U}(1)/\mathbb{Z}_2
\cong\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, every spin<sup>c</sup> structure induces a [[Principal U(1)-bundle|principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundle]] or equivalently a complex [[line bundle]].

== Properties ==

* Every spin structure induces a canonical spin<sup>c</sup> structure.<ref>Mellor 1995, Theorem 2</ref><ref name=":132">Nicolaescu, Example 1.3.16</ref> The reverse implication doesn't hold as the [[complex projective plane]] <math>\mathbb{C}P^2</math> shows.
* Every spin<sup>c</sup> structure induces a canonical spin<sup>h</sup> structure. The reverse implication doesn't hold as the [[Wu manifold]] <math>\operatorname{SU}(3)/\operatorname{SO}(3)</math> shows.{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}
* An orientable manifold <math>M</math> has a spin<sup>c</sup> structure iff its third integral Stiefel–Whitney class <math>W_3(M)
\in H^3(M,\mathbb{Z})</math> vanishes. This class <math>W_3(M)</math> is the image of the second ordinary Stiefel–Whitney class <math>w_2(M)
\in H^2(M,\mathbb{Z}_2)</math> under the Bockstein homomorphism <math>H^2(M,\mathbb{Z}_2)\rightarrow H^3(M,\mathbb{Z})</math>.<ref>Lawson & Michelson 90, Theorem D.2 und Corollary D.4</ref><ref>''Stable complex and Spin<sup>c</sup>-structures'', Proposition D.31</ref>
* Every orientable smooth manifold with four or less dimensions has a spin<sup>c</sup> structure.<ref name=":132" />
* Every [[almost complex manifold]] has a spin<sup>c</sup> structure.<ref>Mellor 1995, Theorem 3</ref><ref name=":132" />
* For a [[Compact space|compact]] spin<sup>c</sup> manifold <math>M</math>, for which a torsion class <math>c\in H^2(M,\mathbb{Z})</math> with <math>w_2(M)=c\operatorname{mod}2</math> exists and which has a Riemannian metric of overall positive scalar curvature, its [[Â genus]] vanishes, hence <math>\widehat{A}(M)=0</math>.<ref>Lawson & Michelson 90, Corollary D.16</ref>

The following properties hold more generally for the lift on the Lie group <math>
\operatorname{Spin}^k(n)
:=\left(
\operatorname{Spin}(n)\times\operatorname{Spin}(k)
\right)/\mathbb{Z}_2
</math>, with the particular case <math>k=2</math> giving:

* If <math>M\times N</math> is a spin<sup>c</sup> manifold, then <math>M</math> and <math>N</math> are spin<sup>c</sup> manifolds.<ref name=":6">Albanese & Milivojević 2021, Proposition 3.6.</ref>
* If <math>M</math> is a spin manifold, then <math>M\times N</math> is a spin<sup>c</sup> manifold iff <math>N</math> is a spin<sup>c</sup> manifold.<ref name=":6" />
* If <math>M</math> and <math>N</math> are spin<sup>c</sup> manifolds of same dimension, then their [[connected sum]] <math>M\# N</math> is a spin<sup>c</sup> manifold.<ref name=":9">Albanese & Milivojević 2021, Proposition 3.7.</ref>
* The following conditions are equivalent:<ref name=":10">Albanese & Milivojević 2021, Proposition 3.2.</ref>
** <math>M</math> is a spin<sup>c</sup> manifold.
** There is a real plane bundle <math>E\twoheadrightarrow M</math>, so that <math>TM\oplus E</math> has a spin structure or equivalently <math>w_2(TM\oplus E)
=0</math>.
** <math>M</math> can be immersed in a spin manifold with two dimensions more.
** <math>M</math> can be embedded in a spin manifold with two dimensions more.

== Cohomology of infinite classifying space ==

The [[cohomology ring]] of the infinite classifying space <math>\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}
:=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c}(n)</math> with coefficients in <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> can be expressed using [[Steenrod square|Steenrod squares]] and [[Wu class|Wu classes]]:<ref>Lawson 2023, p. 8</ref><ref>Hu 2023, Rem. 4.30</ref>
: <math>H^*(\operatorname{BSpin}^\mathrm{c},\mathbb{Z}_2)
\cong H^*(\operatorname{BSO},\mathbb{Z}_2)/(\operatorname{Sq}^1\nu_{2^r},r\geq 1).</math>
